lessons.title: What is Programming?
lessons.simple_explanation: Computers are helpful garden friends, but they need clear instructions to do anything! Programming is simply writing down step-by-step instructions for the computer to follow.
lessons.introduction:
🌟 **The Big Idea:** Computers follow steps in order: Input (what you type) ➔ Process (what the computer does) ➔ Output (what appears on screen).

🔍 **How It Works:** In Python, we use `print()` to send our instructions to the screen. Put your text inside quotation marks `"..."`.

🎯 **Your Secret Tip:** Computers follow instructions exactly. Keep your quotes matching!

discussion.heading: 🌱 The 3 Steps of Every Program
discussion.text:
1. Input: You tell the computer what to do.
2. Process: The computer runs your instructions.
3. Output: The result appears on the screen!

discussion.heading: 🪴 Why Step Order Matters
discussion.text: Just like gardening: you can't harvest seeds before you plant them! Computers always execute instructions in the exact order you write them.

common_mistakes: Forgetting quotation marks: print(Plant seed) will cause an error.
Mismatched quotes: print("Plant seed') does not work.
knowledge_check: What are the 3 main stages of a program? (Input, Process, Output)
Why must instructions be written in the right order?

lessons.title: What is Python?
lessons.simple_explanation: Python is a programming language designed to look and read like plain English. It's one of the friendliest languages in the world to learn!
lessons.introduction:
🌟 **The Big Idea:** Python runs your instructions line-by-line from top to bottom. It is also case-sensitive, meaning capital letters matter!

🔍 **How It Works:** Always write built-in commands like `print()` in lowercase letters.

🎯 **Your Secret Tip:** `Print("Hi")` with a capital P causes an error. Always use lowercase `print()`!

discussion.heading: 🐍 Why Everyone Loves Python
discussion.text: Python is simple, readable, and used all over the world to make websites, build robots, analyze weather data, and create games!

discussion.heading: ⬇️ Sequential Execution
discussion.text: Python reads your code from top to bottom, one line at a time. Line 1 runs first, then Line 2, then Line 3.

code_examples.explanation: Tell the garden that Python is ready to grow:

common_mistakes: Typing Print or PRINT instead of lowercase print.
Missing the closing parenthesis at the end of the line.
knowledge_check: Does Python run code from top to bottom or bottom to top?
Is Print("Hello") the same as print("Hello") in Python?

lessons.title: Leaving Garden Notes
lessons.simple_explanation: Comments are notes for humans! Whenever Python sees a hash symbol (#), it completely ignores that line. Use comments to leave reminders or explain your code.
lessons.introduction:
🌟 **The Big Idea:** Code is read by humans as much as computers! A comment starts with `#` and tells Python: 'Skip this line, it's just a note for me.'

🔍 **How It Works:** Anything after `#` on that line will not run.

🎯 **Your Secret Tip:** If a line of code is causing bugs or isn't needed, you can put `#` in front of it to turn it off!

discussion.heading: 📝 How to Leave a Note
discussion.text:
# This is a garden note
print("This line will print!")
# print("This line will NOT print")

lessons.syntax:
# This is a comment
print("Code runs here")

code_examples.explanation: Using notes while keeping only the message active:
code_examples.code:
# Plant seeds carefully
print("Notes are free")

common_mistakes: Forgetting the # symbol: writing notes without # causes a SyntaxError.
Expecting comments to appear in the console output (they are completely invisible in the output).
knowledge_check: What symbol starts a comment in Python?
Will a line starting with # show up on the screen when you run it?

lessons.title: Say Hello
lessons.simple_explanation: The print() function is how your Python program speaks! Whatever you put inside the parentheses will be displayed in the terminal console.
lessons.introduction:
🌟 **The Big Idea:** Want to talk to the user or see what your program is doing? Use `print()`!

🔍 **How It Works:** Wrap words in quotes: `print("Hello, garden!")`. Numbers don't need quotes: `print(25)`.

🎯 **Your Secret Tip:** You can print multiple things separated by commas: `print("Seeds:", 10)` adds a space automatically!

discussion.heading: 💬 Words vs Numbers
discussion.text:
- Words (Strings) MUST have quotation marks: print("Rose")
- Numbers do NOT need quotes: print(5)

code_examples.explanation: Say hello to your garden sprout:

common_mistakes: Leaving off the quotes around words: print(Hello).
Forgetting the closing parenthesis: print("Hello".
knowledge_check: Do numbers require quotation marks inside print()?
What happens if you forget quotes around words in print()?

lessons.title: Name Your Water
lessons.simple_explanation: A variable is like a labeled jar in your garden shed! You give the jar a name, put a value inside with the equals sign (=), and use it anytime later.
lessons.introduction:
🌟 **The Big Idea:** Variables store information so you don't have to keep retyping it. `water = 4` stores the number 4 under the name `water`.

🔍 **How It Works:** `print(water)` opens the jar and displays `4`! But `print("water")` in quotes just displays the word 'water'.

🎯 **Your Secret Tip:** Don't put quotation marks around variable names when printing their stored value!

discussion.heading: 🏷️ How Assignment Works
discussion.text:
Variable Name on the left, = in the middle, Value on the right:
water = 4
plant = "Sunflower"

discussion.heading: 🔄 Updating a Variable
discussion.text:
You can change what's inside the jar at any time:
water = 4
water = water + 2  # Now water is 6!

code_examples.explanation: Store water containers and print the count:

common_mistakes: Putting quotes around the variable: print("water") prints the word instead of 4.
Starting a variable name with a number: 2water is invalid, use water2 instead.
knowledge_check: What symbol is used to store a value into a variable? (=)
What is the difference between print(water) and print("water")?

lessons.title: Label Your Plant
lessons.simple_explanation: Any text in Python is called a 'string' because characters are strung together! Always wrap your text inside quotation marks.
lessons.introduction:
🌟 **The Big Idea:** Plant labels, messages, and names are all strings. You can store words in variables and even glue strings together with `+`!

🔍 **How It Works:** `crop = "Sunflower"` stores the word Sunflower. You can print it with `print(crop)`.

🎯 **Your Secret Tip:** `20 + 5` does math (`25`), but `"20" + "5"` joins the text (`"205"`)!

discussion.heading: 🔗 Joining Strings (Concatenation)
discussion.text:
first = "Python"
second = "Garden"
print(first + " " + second)  # Prints: Python Garden

discussion.heading: 📏 Measuring Length with len()
discussion.text:
The len() function counts how many letters are in a word:
len("Rose") is 4!

common_mistakes: Forgetting quotes: crop = Sunflower treats Sunflower as an undefined variable.
Forgetting a space when joining strings: "Hello" + "World" becomes "HelloWorld".
knowledge_check: What data type is "Sunflower" in Python? (String)
What does the len() function do?

lessons.title: Count the Seeds
lessons.simple_explanation: Python is an incredible calculator! Use + to add, - to subtract, * to multiply, and / to divide.
lessons.introduction:
🌟 **The Big Idea:** Need to figure out how many seeds you need? Python calculates math instantly.

🔍 **How It Works:** In Python, the asterisk `*` is the multiplication symbol (not the letter x).

🎯 **Your Secret Tip:** If you have 6 seeds per pot and 3 pots: `seeds * pots` gives you `18`!

discussion.heading: ➗ The Math Symbols
discussion.text:
+ Addition (5 + 3 = 8)
- Subtraction (10 - 4 = 6)
* Multiplication (6 * 3 = 18)
/ Division (12 / 3 = 4.0)
// Floor Division (drops decimals: 10 // 3 = 3)
% Remainder (10 % 3 = 1)

common_mistakes: Typing 6 x 3 instead of 6 * 3.
Dividing by zero (causes a ZeroDivisionError).
knowledge_check: Which symbol does Python use for multiplication? (*)
What is the result of 6 * 3 in Python?

lessons.title: Sunny or Not?
lessons.simple_explanation: Code can make smart decisions! An if statement checks if something is true. If it is, Python runs your instructions; otherwise, the else block runs.
lessons.introduction:
🌟 **The Big Idea:** Does your garden have enough sunlight? `if sun > 5:` means 'if the sun is bright, grow!'. `else:` means 'otherwise, wait!'.

🔍 **How It Works:** Always put a colon `:` at the end of the `if` and `else` lines, and indent the code underneath by 4 spaces.

🎯 **Your Secret Tip:** Indentation tells Python which instructions belong inside the decision!

discussion.heading: ☀️ Making a Choice
⚖️ Comparison Symbols
discussion.text:
> greater than
< less than
== equal to (use two equals signs when comparing!)
!= not equal to

common_mistakes: Forgetting the colon : at the end of if and else lines.
Forgetting to indent the code underneath by 4 spaces.
Using = instead of == to compare values.
knowledge_check: What keyword provides the alternative when an if condition is false? (else)
How many spaces of indentation are standard in Python? (4 spaces)

lessons.title: Water Every Plant
lessons.simple_explanation: Don't repeat yourself! A loop tells Python to repeat an action as many times as you want automatically.
lessons.introduction:
🌟 **The Big Idea:** If you have 100 plants to water, you don't want to type 100 lines of code! A `for` loop does the repetition for you.

🔍 **How It Works:** `range(plant_count)` repeats once for each plant. If `plant_count` is 3, it counts `0, 1, 2`; adding `+ 1` displays `1, 2, 3`.

🎯 **Your Secret Tip:** Change `plant_count` to repeat the task for a different number of plants. Put what you want to repeat indented inside the loop!

discussion.heading: 🔄 The for Loop Pattern
discussion.text:
plant_count = 3
for i in range(plant_count):
    print("Water plant", i + 1)

This runs the print statement once for each plant. Change plant_count to use a different garden size.

lessons.syntax:
for i in range(plant_count):
    print("Water plant", i + 1)

code_examples.output:
Water plant 1
Water plant 2
Water plant 3

common_mistakes: Remembering that range(plant_count) starts at 0, not 1.
Forgetting the colon : after range(plant_count).
Forgetting to indent the instruction inside the loop.
knowledge_check: If plant_count is 3, how many times will range(plant_count) run? (3 times)
If plant_count is 5, what numbers does range(plant_count) produce? (0, 1, 2, 3, 4)

lessons.title: Seed Basket
lessons.simple_explanation: A list is like a seed basket that holds multiple items in a specific order using square brackets [].
lessons.introduction:
🌟 **The Big Idea:** Instead of creating 10 separate variables for 10 plants, put them all in one list: `basket = ["Rose", "Mint", "Fern"]`.

🔍 **How It Works:** Python lists start counting at 0! `basket[0]` is Rose, and `basket[1]` is Mint.

🎯 **Your Secret Tip:** Index 0 is the 1st item, index 1 is the 2nd item!

discussion.heading: 🧺 How Lists Work
discussion.text:
basket = ["Rose", "Mint", "Fern"]
print(basket[0])  # Rose (first item)
print(basket[1])  # Mint (second item)
print(basket[2])  # Fern (third item)

discussion.heading: ➕ Adding More Plants
discussion.text:
You can add more items anytime with append:
basket.append("Sunflower")

code_examples.explanation: Pick the second plant from your seed basket:

common_mistakes: Using round parentheses () instead of square brackets [] (that makes a tuple, not a list).
Off-by-one error: basket[1] is the SECOND item, not the first.
knowledge_check: What kind of brackets are used to create a list? ([ ])
What is the index of the very first item in a Python list? (0)
